problem: Multi-billion-parameter Large Action Models (VLAs such as OpenVLA-7B) exceed edge memory and latency budgets, and static quantization/PEFT still spends the same compute depth on easy and hard navigation states.
motivation: Edge robots have roughly 8 GB memory and 200 ms latency budgets, while LAMs need far more, which creates collision risk. Many navigation steps (e.g. straight hallways) are low-uncertainty and do not need full depth, so content-aware adaptive computation should save compute.
key_idea: Combine 4-bit NF4 QLoRA quantization of a VLA backbone with entropy-thresholded multi-exit heads at layers 6/12/18, so confident steps exit early and ambiguous steps use full depth.
insight: The ablation shows the two parts are complementary: QLoRA gives the memory reduction (16.2 to 5.4 GB) and DEE gives the extra latency reduction (120 to 78 ms; DEE alone on FP16 only reaches 285 ms). The threshold sweep shows a clear speed-safety trade-off: at tau of about 0.75 the exit ratio is about 45%, whereas high tau drops SR below 70%. Multi-exit (6/12/18) beats single-exit configurations. Caveat: the results look idealized and the paper contains internal inconsistencies, which weakens confidence in the numbers.
method: QLoRA backbone: OpenVLA-7B weights quantized to block-wise NF4 and frozen, with LoRA (r=64, alpha=16, query/value projections, about 4.5M trainable parameters) fine-tuned on MP3D ObjectNav.
Exit heads: 2-layer MLP (hidden 256, about 1.4M parameters) attached at transformer layers 6, 12 and 18, projecting the hidden state to the discrete action space.

Dynamic early exit: compute Shannon entropy of each head's action distribution and return the argmax action at the first layer with H <= tau; otherwise run to full depth. tau is calibrated on a validation set (about 0.75).
Multi-exit training loss: L_total = L_final + sum_k alpha_k L_exit,k, where each term is cross-entropy against the ground-truth action and alpha_k decreases with depth.
Deployment: TensorRT compilation (layer fusion, kernel auto-tuning), evaluated on hardware emulating a Jetson Orin AGX.

numbers_note: Numbers are self-reported on a custom 1,000-episode MP3D ObjectNav setting with emulated edge hardware, not the standard Habitat challenge protocol. The paper has inconsistencies (FP16 memory given as 28 GB in text vs 16.2 GB in table; TURN 15° vs 30°; the 66.7% memory reduction and the 17.9% latency claim are internally inconsistent).
results: EdgeNav-QE cuts latency by 82.7% (450 to 78 ms) and memory by 66.7% (16.2 to 5.4 GB) versus FP16 OpenVLA-7B, at SR 81.8% versus 84.1%. It beats DeeR-VLA (INT8 + static exit, 95 ms, 81.0% SR) on latency and INT8 PTQ (210 ms, 79.2% SR) on both latency and SR.
limitations: Simulation only with emulated Jetson hardware; no real-robot or Sim2Real validation.
Premature exits are the dominant failure mode (42%), and the paper reports a fixed entropy threshold tau with no adaptive scene-complexity estimate.
Non-standard evaluation, internally inconsistent figures and few comparisons to established ObjectNav methods.
